items.prompt: Why can a person jump back from a sudden loud noise before they've consciously registered what caused it?

options.label: A small structure gets a rough, fast copy of the sensory signal and can trigger a reaction before slower, detailed processing finishes
options.feedback: That structure receives a quick, rough version of the signal along a short pathway, well before the fuller, slower route has finished making sense of it.

options.label: The ears process danger directly, without involving the brain at all
options.feedback: The ears only pick up sound; deciding that something is dangerous and reacting to it still happens in the brain, just very quickly.

options.label: Loud noises bypass the nervous system and act straight on the muscles
options.feedback: Muscles don't respond to sound directly. A nervous signal still has to travel through the brain to trigger the reaction.

options.label: The reaction happens after full conscious recognition of the sound, just very quickly
options.feedback: The jump happens before full conscious recognition, driven by a rough fast pathway rather than by complete conscious processing.

items.ok_line: A rough copy, fast enough to move before you know why.
items.ko_line: Ask which pathway gets the signal first: the fast, rough one or the slow, detailed one.
items.exp_title: A fast, rough copy beats the detailed report
items.exp_text: A signal from the senses travels toward the brain along two routes at once: a short, quick one that reaches a small emotion-processing structure with a rough, low-detail version of the signal, and a longer one that carries a fuller, more accurate version to the thinking regions at the front of the brain. The short route gets there first, and if it looks even roughly like danger, that structure can trigger a reaction immediately, without waiting for the slower, more careful route to catch up. The detailed understanding of what actually happened arrives afterward, once the longer route finishes its work.

items.prompt: Why does a racing heart and sweating so often go along with a sudden burst of fear?

options.label: The brain signals glands to release a hormone that primes the body for quick physical action
options.feedback: That hormone speeds up the heart and triggers sweating as part of readying the body for sudden physical effort.

options.label: Fear directly heats the blood, which the body then tries to cool through sweat
options.feedback: Fear doesn't heat the blood. The sweating is triggered by a hormone signal preparing the body for action, not by a change in blood temperature.

options.label: The heart and skin react on their own, independent of any brain signal
options.feedback: Neither the heart rate change nor the sweating happens on its own; both are triggered by a signal that starts in the brain.

options.label: Sweating happens first and causes the racing heart as a side effect
options.feedback: Sweating doesn't drive the heart rate; both are separate results of the same hormone signal released at roughly the same time.

items.ok_line: One hormone signal, priming the whole body at once.
items.ko_line: Think about what single signal could explain both the racing heart and the sweating together.
items.exp_title: One signal, readying the whole body
items.exp_text: Once the brain judges a situation as threatening, it sends a signal to a pair of small glands that respond by releasing a hormone into the bloodstream. That hormone reaches the heart and makes it beat faster and harder, while also reaching sweat glands in the skin and triggering them to become more active. Both changes serve the same purpose: readying the body to run or to fight before the danger gets any closer.

items.prompt: Why can a person sense that something feels wrong in a situation before they can explain what tipped them off?

options.label: The fast emotional pathway can flag a threat before the slower, reasoning pathway finishes working out the details
options.feedback: The quick route can raise an alarm well before the careful, detail-checking route has pieced together an explanation to go with it.

options.label: Gut feelings come from the stomach sensing danger directly
options.feedback: The stomach doesn't detect danger on its own; any bodily sensation follows a signal that starts in the brain, not the other way around.

options.label: The feeling appears only after the reasoning pathway has already worked out what's wrong
options.feedback: It's the reverse: the uneasy feeling tends to arrive first, from the fast pathway, before the slower reasoning pathway supplies an explanation.

options.label: There is no real difference in speed between the two pathways
options.feedback: One pathway is deliberately short and rough for speed, while the other is longer and more thorough, and that speed difference is exactly the point.

items.ok_line: The alarm sounds before the explanation is ready.
items.ko_line: Think about which arrives first: the uneasy feeling, or the reason behind it.
items.exp_title: The alarm arrives before the explanation
items.exp_text: The same fast, rough pathway that can trigger a flinch at a sudden noise can also register a subtler pattern, something slightly off in a face or a situation, and raise a feeling of unease about it. That feeling can arrive well before the slower, more careful pathway has gathered enough detail to say exactly what's wrong. So the sense that something is off often shows up first, with the reasoning behind it only catching up afterward.

items.prompt: Why does deliberately copying someone's smile tend to make a person feel a little more cheerful themselves?

options.label: Signals from the moving facial muscles feed back to the brain and nudge its emotional state
options.feedback: The brain reads signals coming back from the face, and those signals can shift its emotional state, not just express one already there.

options.label: Smiling releases a hormone that lowers heart rate no matter how a person feels inside
options.feedback: It isn't about heart rate here; the effect runs through signals from the facial muscles feeding back to the brain's emotional processing.

options.label: Facial expressions are purely an output with no path leading back to the brain
options.feedback: There is a path leading back: signals from the moving muscles do feed information to the brain, which is exactly why the effect happens at all.

options.label: The effect only works if the smile is completely genuine to begin with
options.feedback: The feedback signal comes from the muscles being used, whether or not the smile started out as a genuine one.

items.ok_line: The face reports back, and the brain listens.
items.ko_line: Ask whether a facial expression only sends signals outward, or whether some come back to the brain too.
items.exp_title: The face reports back to the brain
items.exp_text: Moving the muscles used in a genuine smile sends sensory signals back up to brain regions involved in processing emotion, not just outward to be seen by others. Those returning signals get folded into the brain's own read of its current emotional state, nudging it slightly in the direction the expression suggests. A face isn't only a display of a feeling that's already there; it's also a channel that feeds information back the other way.

items.prompt: How does the brain manage to calm down an alarm reaction once a situation turns out to be safe?

options.label: A region at the front of the brain assesses the situation and sends signals that dampen the alarm structure's activity
options.feedback: Once that front region concludes there's no real danger, it sends signals that quiet the alarm structure back down.

options.label: The alarm reaction simply fades on its own after a fixed length of time, with no brain involvement
options.feedback: The calming down isn't automatic or timed; it happens because a specific region actively assesses the situation and sends a dampening signal.

options.label: A hormone released earlier eventually breaks down and that alone causes the calm
options.feedback: The hormone's decline plays a part in the body's response, but the alarm structure itself is calmed by an active signal from the front of the brain, not by that alone.

options.label: The senses simply stop sending any signal once the danger has passed
options.feedback: The senses keep sending signals as normal; what changes is that a front brain region actively works to quiet the alarm response.

items.ok_line: A reasoned all-clear, sent down to quiet the alarm.
items.ko_line: Think about what has to actively step in to override an alarm, rather than what fades away by itself.
items.exp_title: A reasoned all-clear from the front of the brain
items.exp_text: The alarm structure reacts to rough, fast information and can't tell on its own whether a threat is real or not. A region at the front of the brain, working with the fuller, more detailed picture that arrives a little later, weighs the situation and, if it judges things safe, sends signals back that actively suppress the alarm structure's activity. The racing heart and the tension ease only once that reasoned all-clear has been sent.

items.prompt: Why does a burst of stress hormone in the blood not just keep climbing higher and higher during a stressful event?

options.label: Rising levels of the hormone signal back to the brain to reduce further release, in a loop that limits how high it climbs
options.feedback: Once the hormone level rises enough, it signals the brain to dial back further release, keeping the surge from climbing without limit.

options.label: The glands that release the hormone simply run out of material after a short burst
options.feedback: The glands aren't running dry; the level is actively kept in check by a signal fed back to the brain, not by supply running out.

options.label: The hormone breaks itself down the instant it's released, with no feedback involved
options.feedback: Breakdown of the hormone does happen, but the level is also actively controlled by a feedback signal to the brain, which is the more direct brake on further release.

options.label: Stress hormone levels are fixed and never actually rise during a stressful event
options.feedback: The level does rise once a stressful event begins; what's being explained here is why it doesn't keep climbing without limit.

items.ok_line: A rising level signals its own brake.
items.ko_line: Think about what a rising hormone level could tell the brain about whether to keep releasing more.
items.exp_title: A brake triggered by the hormone itself
items.exp_text: As the stress hormone builds up in the bloodstream, it travels back to the brain and acts on regions that control its own release, signalling that enough has been produced for now. Those regions respond by reducing the signal that had been driving further release from the glands. The level climbs sharply at first and then levels off and falls back, checked by a brake that the hormone itself switches on.

items.prompt: How can a quick 'gut feeling' about a choice sometimes lead to a better decision than working through it step by step?

options.label: Past outcomes are paired with bodily feelings that get triggered again and quietly bias a new decision
options.feedback: A situation resembling a past one can trigger the bodily feeling tied to how that past choice turned out, nudging the decision before any conscious weighing begins.

options.label: Gut feelings are generated completely at random, independent of any past experience
options.feedback: They aren't random; they draw on bodily feelings linked to how similar situations turned out before, which is what gives them any value at all.

options.label: The stomach itself works out the best choice and sends the answer to the brain
options.feedback: The stomach doesn't calculate anything. The feeling originates in the brain's linking of past outcomes to bodily states, not in the stomach itself.

options.label: A gut feeling only ever appears after a decision has already been made
options.feedback: The feeling shows up before or during the decision, nudging it, rather than only appearing in hindsight after the choice is already settled.

items.ok_line: An old outcome, replayed as a feeling, nudging the new choice.
items.ko_line: Ask where the feeling behind a hunch actually comes from, rather than treating it as something that appears from nowhere.
items.exp_title: An old outcome, replayed as a feeling
items.exp_text: Choices that turned out badly or well in the past leave behind not just a memory of what happened, but a paired bodily feeling: a tightening, a lift, a wariness. When a new situation resembles one of those past choices, that paired feeling can be triggered again before any deliberate weighing-up has even started, tilting a person toward or away from an option. A hunch, in that sense, is the compressed residue of past outcomes showing up early, ahead of any reasoning.

items.prompt: Why can genuine emotional tears look and feel different from tears caused by chopping an onion?

options.label: Emotional tears are triggered through a different neural pathway and carry a different chemical makeup than reflex tears
options.feedback: A signal from emotional brain regions drives this kind of tear, and what it carries differs from the tears a simple physical irritant produces.

options.label: There is no real difference between the two kinds of tears at all
options.feedback: The two are triggered by different pathways and carry a different chemical makeup, which is exactly why they aren't the same.

options.label: Emotional tears come only from the left eye
options.feedback: Which eye tears from has nothing to do with the difference; the real distinction is in the triggering pathway and the tear's makeup.

options.label: Reflex tears are produced by the brain, while emotional tears are produced by the eye alone
options.feedback: It's the other way around in terms of what's distinctive: emotional tears are specifically driven by brain regions handling feeling, more so than the simple local reflex is.

items.ok_line: A different pathway, carrying a different mix.
items.ko_line: Think about what triggers each kind of tear, and whether that trigger might change what's actually in them.
items.exp_title: A different trigger, a different mix
items.exp_text: An irritant like onion vapour triggers tears through a simple local reflex, a direct response to something physically stinging the eye. An intense emotional state instead engages brain regions that process feeling, and those regions send their own signal down to the tear glands, producing tears that carry a different chemical makeup than the reflex kind. Two very different routes lead to the same glands, and the tears that come out are not quite the same substance.

items.prompt: Why is it so hard to stay furious and feel calm and relaxed at the same moment?

options.label: The calming system and the alarm-arousal system inhibit each other, so one tends to dominate at a time
options.feedback: The two systems work against each other, so strong activity in one tends to suppress the other rather than letting both run fully at once.

options.label: Anger and calm are processed in completely separate brains that never interact
options.feedback: Both draw on the same nervous system; the reason they clash is that the two systems they rely on actively suppress each other, not that they're isolated from each other.

options.label: The body can only handle one emotion at a time due to a limit on hormones available
options.feedback: It isn't a hormone shortage; it's that the calming and alarm systems actively work against each other, so one tends to win out.

options.label: Calm and anger are actually the exact same bodily state, just labelled differently
options.feedback: They involve opposite patterns of activity in the nervous system, not the same state under a different name, which is exactly why they conflict.

items.ok_line: Two systems pulling opposite ways, and one usually wins.
items.ko_line: Think about whether the calming system and the alarm system could both be running at full strength together.
items.exp_title: Two systems that hold each other back
items.exp_text: One branch of the nervous system drives the racing heart and tension of anger, readying the body for confrontation, while an opposing branch slows the heart and eases muscles when a situation is safe. Strong activity in either branch tends to actively suppress the other, rather than the two simply running side by side. A body driven hard by the alarm branch has very little room left for the calming branch to take hold at the same moment.

items.prompt: Why does putting a strong feeling into words often make that feeling less overwhelming?

options.label: Naming the feeling engages a front region of the brain that in turn quiets the alarm structure driving the feeling
options.feedback: Working out the right word for a feeling activates that front region, and its activity sends a dampening signal back to the alarm structure.

options.label: Saying a feeling out loud makes the stress hormone disappear from the blood instantly
options.feedback: The hormone doesn't vanish the moment something is said aloud; the effect works through brain activity that gradually dampens the alarm response, not an instant chemical change.

options.label: Naming an emotion has no measurable effect on brain activity at all
options.feedback: Naming an emotion does engage a specific front region of the brain, and that activity is what feeds back to ease the alarm response.

options.label: Talking about a feeling only helps because another person hears it and offers comfort
options.feedback: The effect shows up even without anyone else listening, since it comes from the brain activity involved in finding the words, not from another person's reaction.

items.ok_line: Finding the word engages a region that talks the alarm down.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens inside the brain during the effort of finding the right word, not about who else might hear it.
items.exp_title: Finding the word talks the alarm down
items.exp_text: Searching for the precise word for a feeling calls on a region toward the front of the brain, the same kind of region involved in reasoning through a situation and weighing it up. Activity in that region sends signals that dampen the alarm structure generating the feeling in the first place, the same way judging a situation safe would. Simply finding the right word, then, is itself a small act of reasoning that reaches back and quiets the feeling it's describing.
